extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and policy-readers interested in the history and practice of scholarly peer review (historians of science, journal editors, research administrators)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes historical norms, purposes, and practical standards used to evaluate and operate peer review for journals and grant bodies; useful for understanding what counts as valid review practices and why different practices have been adopted or criticized. Emphasizes roles (referee/adviser/gatekeeper), anonymity, selection of reviewers, and reforms (signed/open review, preprints, consensus models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: peer review as expert vetting and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is the process by which articles and applications are vetted by experts in a researcher’s field, meant to provide validation and quality control and often considered a marker of objective scientific inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate both publications and grant proposals; historically became a central expectation only in the 20th century. The article frames peer review as intended to ensure quality/trustworthiness, though its efficacy is debated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity/confidentiality of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee reports became confidential documents and the author would not know who the referees were or what they said; secrecy was justified on grounds that referees could not offer candid feedback otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Royal Society practice of confidential reports; NSF controversy in 1970s where some demanded full disclosure but NSF defended confidentiality. Reform proposals include signed reports; trade-offs: candidness vs accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role expectation — adviser versus gatekeeper
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees were originally expected to advise editors—flagging embarrassing or discrediting material—whereas later they came to be seen as gatekeepers responsible for the quality of the scientific literature as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: the remit of reviewers can be limited (advice) or decisive (accept/reject). Historical shift led to concentration of power among a small group of prominent scientists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial control versus systematic external refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors sometimes made accept/reject decisions without external referees; using referees was often a logistical choice (speed, recruitment of content) rather than an epistemological necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial journals like Nature and Philosophical Magazine relied on editorial staff for decades; editors preferred to recruit content and avoid delays from referee reports. Not using referees did not preclude publishing important work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal society review versus external anonymous review
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal learned-society vetting (members commenting in committee or publicly) differed in purpose and form from external anonymous refereeing: it aimed to safeguard the society’s reputation and tended to be communal and non-anonymous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Académie des Sciences vetting, Royal Society internal discussion. Such internal review typically lacked anonymity and was not intended to function as modern gatekeeping peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and publication speed versus consultation of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritizing rapid publication (e.g., Académie des Sciences, commercial weeklies) often led to avoiding outside referees to prevent delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals valuing fast/regular schedules sometimes eschewed referees entirely. Trade-off: speed and editorial recruitment versus the slower process of outside review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who counts as a 'peer' — narrowness of acceptable reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'peer review' implies that only a narrow range of expert peers—those with disciplinary standing comparable to the author—are permitted to evaluate work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The renaming from 'refereeing' to 'peer review' limited acceptable reviewers and helped bind assessment of quality to a bounded community of experts; this has implications for diversity of perspectives in review.

rubrics_metrics.name: External refereeing for funding bodies versus in-house panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding organizations varied: some used external referees, others used in-house panels or employees to evaluate proposals; practices influenced by trust, accountability, and scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: NSF used external referees since 1950 and faced Congressional scrutiny; NIH used in-house study sections. Choice affects perceptions of fairness and scientific autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee remit: utility/embarrassment versus truth/value judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier conceptions had referees flag material that might embarrass or discredit a publication rather than making judgments about the truth or novelty of the findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for modern reviewers: scope may include checking for scandalous/harmful content and fitness for publication, not only scientific correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective use of referees (editorial discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors often sent papers to referees when a paper seemed questionable; papers the editor liked were sometimes not sent for external opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This selective refereeing means referee input has historically been used as justification for rejection rather than as a routine step for all submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee composition and concentration of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on a small number of prominent scientists for refereeing concentrated power in an elite inner circle that could shape a journal’s contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: over-reliance on an elite group risks homogenizing accepted work and reinforcing gatekeeping biases; diversification of reviewers is a countermeasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as marker of scientific legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: By the mid- to late-20th century peer review became synonymous with scientific respectability; institutions without systematic peer review were seen as shoddy or unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: peer review is treated as essential to grant-making and publishing legitimacy; this historical sedimentation makes reform politically and culturally difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias and fairness concerns (gender, race, nepotism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical work has indicated that women and underrepresented minorities are more likely to receive unfavorable referee reports; nepotism and sexism have been documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited: Wennerås & Wold (1997); Bornmann et al. (2007); Ginther et al. (2011). Implication: systems should be assessed and redesigned to mitigate bias (e.g., blinding, reviewer training, diverse reviewer pools).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review may suppress innovation and favor safe projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue peer review suppresses innovative research and rewards more familiar, safer projects that fit existing expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence and concerns motivate discussions of alternative processes to better capture high-risk/high-reward work (e.g., different grant structures, open review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open/signed review versus anonymous review (reform proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals that referees should sign their reports argue that signed reviews will be more thoughtful and constructive than anonymous comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical echo: Whewell’s early idea and Conlan’s proposal for NSF; trade-offs include accountability and potential reduction in candid feedback. Some journals experiment with partial openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community open-feedback / preprints as alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative model is to eschew formal peer review and allow researchers to post their papers for feedback from the whole community (example: arXiv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model emphasizes broad community critique and rapid dissemination but raises questions about quality filtering, credit, and archival validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-referee consensus decision model
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals (e.g., eLife) solicit opinions from multiple referees but have referees and the editor discuss the paper to arrive at a single unanimous decision rather than sending multiple separate reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This collaborative model can produce clearer editorial guidance and reduce conflicting reviewer signals to authors; it's an example of experimental variation in peer review practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and oversight of review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions may create oversight or audit mechanisms to ensure that referee reports—both positive and negative—are taken into account in final decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: NSF hearings in 1975 led to more weight being placed on referee opinions and creation of an audit office; oversight can increase transparency and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based assessment of peer review effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little solid evidence on peer review’s efficacy; calls exist for measuring how well peer review distinguishes good science from bad and for studying its strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited reports: 2011 UK Parliament report; studies that examine retractions, reproducibility, and gatekeeping effectiveness. Implication: reform should be informed by empirical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical contingency: peer review is not timeless and can be reformed
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review emerged in specific historical circumstances (rise of journal-centric publishing, Cold War funding dynamics) and therefore is changeable rather than a fixed, ancient institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument used to counter the myth that peer review is an unchangeable feature of science; supports openness to experimenting with models (signed review, preprints, consensus review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose evolution: credit/priority versus quality assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: The purposes attached to publication and review shifted over time—from communicating results and establishing priority to enforcing publication in reputable, peer-reviewed journals as a form of credit and quality assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding this evolution helps evaluate whether current review practices serve contemporary aims (credit allocation, public accountability, reproducibility) and may suggest areas for reform.
